title: The 60-Minute Mental Marathon Part II: SEND
author: Joel Kenyon
summary: A secondary science teacher and head of department continues his series on teacher cognitive load, this time aimed at the volume of special-needs documentation now landing on classroom teachers in England. He opens with the numbers: SEND identification up a third in a decade, EHCPs doubled as a share of pupils, and in his own deprived area close to one in four secondary pupils on the register. Against that he sets the arithmetic of compliance, including a colleague holding more than seventy pupil passports and twenty EHCPs, which at three minutes apiece is over four hours of reading before a single lesson is planned. His sharpest move is to reject the standard reply that teachers simply need more training. He argues he has had more SEND training than training on anything else, and that the real problem is the content of the documents, which routinely prescribe coloured overlays, comic sans, fidget toys, learning styles and no questioning, none of which survive contact with the evidence. He is careful not to blame parents, who quite reasonably fight for what is written on the page, and instead puts the burden on the people writing these plans. The piece closes on the time-neutrality principle from Part I: if something is added, something must go, and what is currently going is classroom instruction itself.
points: The critique targets the documents rather than the pupils or the parents, arguing that plans prescribing debunked interventions cannot be trusted on the rest of their content either.
A concrete workload calculation, seventy-plus passports and twenty EHCPs at three minutes each, converts an abstract inclusion duty into more than four hours of pre-lesson reading.
The author dismantles the reflexive call for more SEND training by noting it is already the most heavily trained topic in his professional life, which redirects the problem toward document quality.

Several commonly prescribed adjustments are shown to work against inclusion in practice, notably exit passes that let a pupil opt out during new instruction and instructions not to question the pupil who most needs checking.

He argues the coloured-overlay recommendation reveals a category error about dyslexia, treating a phonological processing difficulty as an optical one and so withholding the intervention that would help.
quotes: Nationally, the percentage of SEND pupils has increased 33% in the last decade and those with an EHCP has increased from 2.8% to 6% over the same time period.
The amount of information that a teacher must digest and compute in one 60-minute lesson is far too much cognitive load.
The demand of the guidance in SEND passports and ECHPs has become so overwhelming that one of my friends who is an RE teacher, has more than 70 pupil passports and 20 EHCPs to read.
If we take the conservative estimate of 3 minutes per ECHP or Pupil Passport, this can account for over 4 hours just reading these documents.
It should not take a teacher to know what is and what isn't evidence backed to be able to effectively implement the advice of these EHCPs. This again is too much workload and far too much to process.

Dyslexia is a phonological processing disorder, not an optical defect. If a pupil does not understand a phoneme, or confuses one for another, putting it in blue is not going to magically give them that understanding.

Good routines, regular checks for understanding, expectations made clear, instructions front loaded, information delivered in a way all pupils can learn. This is what the main focus should be, not all the gimmicks that make it look like we are being inclusive when in reality we are setting SEND students up to fail.
